about: 1P3 is a Part IA course in Cambridge's Engineering Tripos. On the 2025–26 syllabus page (the 2026–27 page could not be checked) it has 12 lectures in two six-lecture parts, in Michaelmas and Lent: Physical Principles of Electronics (charge, fields, Gauss's law, capacitance, current and resistance, magnetic fields, Faraday's law and inductance) and Electromagnetics (images, energy and virtual work in electrostatic systems, then magnetic materials, magnetic circuits and permanent magnets). The syllabus stresses physical understanding with simple maths and sensible approximations. It is examined in Paper 3 (Electrical and Information Engineering), a 3-hour paper shared with Analysis of Circuits and Devices and Digital Circuits and Information Processing.
topics: Charge, Coulomb's law and the electric field
Electric flux density, Gauss's law and potential
Capacitance and AC behaviour of capacitors
Magnetic fields of currents: Biot–Savart and Ampère
Flux linkage, Faraday's law and inductance
Electrostatic systems: images, energy and virtual work
Permanent magnets, magnetic energy and forces

notes.h: Charge, Coulomb's law and the electric field
notes.body:
1P3 opens with the physics behind resistors, capacitors and inductors. The emphasis, as the syllabus says, is physical understanding with simple maths: superposition, dot and cross products, and sensible approximations.

Charge
- Charge is quantised in units of e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and is conserved.
- Like charges repel, unlike charges attract. Conductors let charge move freely; insulators (dielectrics) do not.

Coulomb's law
- The force between point charges q₁ and q₂ a distance r apart in a vacuum is F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²), along the line joining them.
- ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, so 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
- Forces from several charges add as vectors (superposition).

Electric field
- The electric field E is the force per unit positive test charge: E = F/q, in V/m (equivalently N/C).
- Point charge Q: E = Q/(4πε₀r²), pointing radially away from a positive charge.
- Infinite line charge λ (C/m): E = λ/(2πε₀r), radial and falling as 1/r.
- Infinite sheet of charge σ (C/m²): E = σ/(2ε₀) on each side, independent of distance.
- These three cases show how the geometry sets the fall-off: 1/r² (point), 1/r (line), constant (plane).

Dielectrics
- In an insulator, an applied field slightly separates the positive and negative charge in each atom or molecule, or aligns existing molecular dipoles. This is polarisation.
- The result is bound "polarisation charge" on the surfaces of the dielectric, which partly cancels the applied field inside it.
- For a linear dielectric we absorb this into the permittivity ε = ε₀εr, where εr is the relative permittivity (about 1.0006 for air, roughly 2–3 for many polymers, around 80 for water at low frequency).
- With a dielectric filling all space, Coulomb's law becomes F = q₁q₂/(4πεr²): the force and field are reduced by εr.

Dielectric breakdown
- Above a certain field strength (the dielectric strength), an insulator conducts, often by an avalanche of ionisation. For air at atmospheric pressure the figure usually quoted is about 3 MV/m.
- Breakdown is why sharp points and thin wires are dangerous at high voltage: the field is highest where the radius of curvature is smallest.

Worked example
Charges +4 μC at x = 0 and +1 μC at x = 0.3 m. The force between them is 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻⁶ × 1 × 10⁻⁶/0.3² ≈ 0.40 N (repulsive). The field is zero between them where 4/x² = 1/(0.3 − x)², i.e. 2(0.3 − x) = x, so x = 0.2 m.

Exam tips: always draw the geometry and the field direction before writing an equation; most errors in field questions are sign or direction errors in the superposition.

notes.h: Electric flux density, Gauss's law and potential
notes.body:
Electric flux density D
- D is defined so that it depends only on the free charge: in a linear, isotropic material D = εE = ε₀εrE. Units are C/m².
- In terms of polarisation P (dipole moment per unit volume), D = ε₀E + P.
- Across a boundary between dielectrics with no free surface charge, the normal component of D is continuous. So where D is normal to the boundary, the field E = D/ε is larger in the material with lower permittivity. This matters for air gaps in insulation.

Gauss's law
- The total flux of D out of any closed surface equals the free charge enclosed: ∮ D · dS = Q_enclosed.
- This is "flux conservation": flux lines start on positive charge and end on negative charge.
- It is most useful when symmetry tells you D is constant in magnitude and normal to a chosen surface:
- Sphere around a point charge: D × 4πr² = Q, so D = Q/(4πr²).
- Cylinder of length l around a line charge: D × 2πrl = λl, so D = λ/(2πr) (no flux through the end caps).
- Pillbox across a charged sheet: D = σ/2 on each side; next to a conductor surface (field on one side only) D = σ.
- Inside a conductor in equilibrium E = 0, so any net charge sits on the surface.

Potential and voltage
- The potential difference between points A and B is the work done per unit charge moving a test charge from B to A against the field: V_A − V_B = −∫ from B to A of E · dl = ∫ from A to B of E · dl.
- Electrostatic fields are conservative, so the result is independent of path. Equivalently E = −∇V: the field points "downhill" in potential.
- Point charge (zero at infinity): V = Q/(4πεr).
- Between coaxial cylinders of radii a < b carrying λ per unit length: V = (λ/2πε) ln(b/a).
- Parallel plates with uniform field: V = Ed.

Worked example: isolated sphere
A conducting sphere of radius R with charge Q has V = Q/(4πε₀R) at its surface, so its capacitance is C = Q/V = 4πε₀R. Even a sphere the size of the Earth (R ≈ 6.37 × 10⁶ m) has C ≈ 7.1 × 10⁻⁴ F, about 0.7 mF, which shows how small "free-space" capacitances are.

Worked example: coaxial line
For inner radius a = 1 mm, outer radius b = 4 mm and V across the dielectric, λ = 2πεV/ln(b/a), and E(r) = V/(r ln(b/a)). The field is greatest at the inner conductor: E_max = V/(a ln(b/a)). For fixed b and V this is smallest when b/a = e (differentiate a ln(b/a) with respect to a), a classic cable-design result.

Exam tips: in Gauss's law questions, state the symmetry, sketch the Gaussian surface, and say which faces carry flux; examiners award marks for the argument, not just the formula.

notes.h: Capacitance and AC behaviour of capacitors
notes.body:
Definition
- Capacitance C = Q/V: the charge stored per volt between two conductors. Units: farads (F).
- To find C: assume charge ±Q, use Gauss's law to find D and hence E, integrate E to find V, then divide.

Standard results
- Parallel plates, area A, separation d, filled with permittivity ε, neglecting fringing: C = εA/d.
- Coaxial cylinders, radii a < b: capacitance per unit length C′ = 2πε/ln(b/a).
- Isolated sphere of radius R: C = 4πεR.

Combinations
- Parallel: capacitances add (same V, charges add).
- Series: reciprocals add (same Q, voltages add): 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
- A capacitor with two dielectric layers stacked between the plates is two capacitors in series; side-by-side dielectrics are in parallel.

Layered dielectric example
Plates of area 0.01 m² have 1 mm of glass (εr = 6) and a 0.1 mm air gap between them, with 1 kV applied.
- C_glass = ε₀ × 6 × 0.01/10⁻³ ≈ 531 pF; C_air = ε₀ × 0.01/10⁻⁴ ≈ 885 pF; in series C ≈ 332 pF.
- D is the same in both layers: D = Q/A = 332 × 10⁻¹² × 1000/0.01 ≈ 3.32 × 10⁻⁵ C/m².
- E_air = D/ε₀ ≈ 3.75 MV/m and E_glass = E_air/6 ≈ 0.63 MV/m. Check: 3.75 × 10⁶ × 10⁻⁴ + 0.625 × 10⁶ × 10⁻³ = 375 + 625 = 1000 V.
- The thin air gap carries more than a third of the voltage and its field exceeds the roughly 3 MV/m breakdown strength of air: it may discharge even though the glass is lightly stressed.

Capacitors in circuits
- Differentiating Q = CV gives i = C dv/dt. A capacitor's voltage cannot change instantaneously (that would need infinite current).
- With sinusoidal signals v = V cos ωt, the current is −ωCV sin ωt, which leads the voltage by 90°.
- In phasor form I = jωC V, so the impedance is Z = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC). The reactance magnitude 1/(ωC) is large at low frequency (open circuit at DC) and small at high frequency.
- A capacitor stores energy ½CV² but dissipates none on average.

Worked example
A capacitor of 3.54 nF (plates 0.01 m², 0.1 mm of εr = 4 dielectric) has reactance 1/(2π × 50 × 3.54 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 900 kΩ at 50 Hz, but only about 45 Ω at 1 MHz.

Exam tips: remember that series dielectric layers share the same D, not the same E; then E = D/ε tells you which layer is most highly stressed.

Current
- Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = dQ/dt, in amperes (C/s).
- Conventional current flows in the direction positive charge would move; in metals the carriers are electrons moving the other way.

Current density
- Current density J is current per unit area (A/m²), a vector in the direction of flow. Through a surface, I = ∫ J · dS.
- If there are n carriers per unit volume, each of charge q, drifting with mean velocity v_d, then J = nqv_d.
- In a conductor the carriers are accelerated by the field and repeatedly scattered, giving a drift velocity proportional to E. This gives the "microscopic" Ohm's law J = σE, where σ is the conductivity (S/m) and ρ = 1/σ the resistivity (Ω m).

Drift velocity example
Copper has roughly 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. For 1 A in a 1 mm² wire, v_d = I/(nqA) = 1/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 7 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, well under a millimetre per second. Signals travel fast because the field propagates, not the electrons.

Resistance
- Integrating J = σE along a uniform bar of length L and area A gives V = EL and I = JA = σEA, so R = V/I = ρL/A. This is the macroscopic Ohm's law V = IR.
- For copper ρ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, so 10 m of 1 mm² wire has R ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ × 10/10⁻⁶ = 0.17 Ω.
- For metals ρ rises with temperature (more lattice vibration, more scattering).
- Power dissipated: P = VI = I²R = V²/R.

Non-uniform geometries
Split the conductor into thin elements in series or parallel, just as for capacitance.
- Leakage between coaxial cylinders (radii a < b, length l) through material of resistivity ρ: current flows radially through shells of area 2πrl, so R = ∫ ρ dr/(2πrl) = ρ ln(b/a)/(2πl).

The capacitance–resistance analogy
- Compare C = εA/d with R = ρd/A for the same parallel-plate geometry: RC = ρε. The same holds for the coaxial case, since C = 2πεl/ln(b/a) and R = ρ ln(b/a)/(2πl).
- This is because both problems solve the same field equations: E-field lines carry D in the capacitor and J in the resistor. Once you know one, you know the other.
- ρε is the time for charge to relax inside a leaky dielectric.

Exam tips: when a wire is stretched at constant volume, A falls as L rises, so R = ρL/A scales with L²; doubling the length quadruples the resistance.

notes.h: Magnetic fields of currents: Biot–Savart and Ampère
notes.body:
Force between current-carrying wires
- Two long parallel wires carrying I₁ and I₂ a distance d apart in air exert a force per unit length F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd). Currents in the same direction attract; opposite directions repel.
- μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m (to a very good approximation), so F/L = 2 × 10⁻⁷ I₁I₂/d. Two 100 A wires 1 m apart feel 2 mN per metre.
- This was the basis of the historical definition of the ampere; since 2019 the ampere has been defined by fixing the value of e.

Magnetic flux density B
- B (tesla) is defined by the force on a moving charge or current element: F = q v × B, and on a wire F = I L × B, magnitude BIL when the wire is perpendicular to B.
- Interpreting the wire-wire force: wire 1 sets up B = μ₀I₁/(2πd) at wire 2, and wire 2 feels BI₂ per metre.

Biot–Savart law
- A short current element I dl produces at distance r a field dB = μ₀I dl × r̂/(4πr²). The field circulates around the current (right-hand grip rule).
- Superposition of elements gives standard results:
- Long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr).
- Centre of a circular loop of radius a: B = μ₀I/(2a); on the axis at distance z, B = μ₀Ia²/[2(a² + z²)^(3/2)].
- Long solenoid with n turns per metre: B = μ₀nI inside, uniform and axial, and approximately zero outside.

Ampère's law
- Around any closed loop, the line integral of B equals μ₀ times the current threading the loop: ∮ B · dl = μ₀I_enclosed (in non-magnetic material).
- With symmetry it gives fields quickly:
- Long wire: B × 2πr = μ₀I, so B = μ₀I/(2πr).
- Inside a solid wire of radius a with uniform current: only the fraction r²/a² is enclosed, so B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²), rising linearly to the surface.
- Toroid with N turns: B = μ₀NI/(2πr) inside the core, zero outside.
- Coaxial cable: B = μ₀I/(2πr) between the conductors and zero outside (the currents cancel).

Worked examples
- 10 A in a long wire: at 5 cm, B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10/0.05 = 4 × 10⁻⁵ T = 40 μT, comparable to the Earth's field.
- Solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carrying 2 A: B = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 2 ≈ 2.5 mT.
- Single loop, radius 0.1 m, 5 A: B at the centre = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 5/0.2 ≈ 31 μT.

Exam tips: Ampère's law is only quick when you can argue that B is constant along the loop and parallel to it; say so explicitly. Otherwise use Biot–Savart and superposition.

notes.h: Flux linkage, Faraday's law and inductance
notes.body:
Magnetic flux and flux linkage
- The flux through a surface is Φ = ∫ B · dS, in webers (Wb). For uniform B normal to area A, Φ = BA.
- Flux lines form closed loops, so the net flux out of any closed surface is zero.
- A coil of N turns, each linking flux Φ, has flux linkage λ = NΦ.

Faraday's law
- A changing flux linkage induces an emf: e = −dλ/dt = −N dΦ/dt.
- The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change that caused it.
- The change can come from a time-varying B (transformer action) or from motion of a conductor through B (motional emf e = Blv for a rod of length l moving at v perpendicular to B).
- Example: a 100-turn coil of area 0.01 m² in which B rises uniformly from 0 to 0.5 T in 0.1 s has |e| = 100 × 0.01 × 0.5/0.1 = 5 V.

Self-inductance
- L = λ/I: flux linkage per amp. Units: henries (H).
- From Faraday, v = L di/dt (taking the voltage drop in the direction of current). Current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously.
- Long solenoid, N turns, length l, area A: B = μ₀NI/l, Φ = BA, λ = NΦ, so L = μ₀N²A/l. Note the N² dependence.
- Example: N = 500, l = 0.25 m, radius 1 cm: L = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 500² × π × 10⁻⁴/0.25 ≈ 0.39 mH.
- Coaxial line (field between conductors only): L′ = (μ₀/2π) ln(b/a) per unit length. With C′ = 2πε/ln(b/a), L′C′ = μ₀ε, independent of geometry.

Mutual inductance
- M = λ₂/I₁: flux linkage in coil 2 per amp in coil 1. It can be shown that M₁₂ = M₂₁.
- Example: a long solenoid with n₁ = 2000 turns/m and area 10⁻³ m², with a 50-turn coil wound on it: M = μ₀n₁N₂A ≈ 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 × 50 × 10⁻³ ≈ 126 μH.
- With a coupling coefficient k (0 ≤ k ≤ 1), M = k√(L₁L₂).

AC behaviour
- With sinusoidal current, V = jωL I: impedance jωL, reactance ωL, and current lags voltage by 90°.
- Reactance rises with frequency: an inductor is a short circuit at DC and blocks high frequencies. A 10 mH inductor has a reactance of about 3.1 Ω at 50 Hz.
- Inductors store energy ½LI² in the magnetic field.

Exam tips: to find any inductance, follow the chain I → B (Ampère or Biot–Savart) → Φ → λ = NΦ → L = λ/I, stating assumptions such as "long solenoid, end effects ignored".

notes.h: Electrostatic systems: images, energy and virtual work
notes.body:
Part 2 of 1P3 revisits electrostatics with more powerful tools.

The method of images
- A grounded conducting plane forces V = 0 on its surface. The field above it is exactly the same as if the plane were removed and replaced by an "image" charge of opposite sign at the mirror-image position.
- This works because the real charge plus image gives V = 0 on the plane, and the solution of an electrostatics problem with given boundary conditions is unique.
- Point charge q at height h above a grounded plane: image −q at depth h. The charge is attracted to the plane with force q²/(4πε₀(2h)²). For q = 1 nC and h = 1 cm this is about 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ N.
- Line charge (e.g. an overhead wire) at height h: image line charge −λ at depth h.
- Wire of radius a at height h above ground (h ≫ a): C′ ≈ 2πε₀/ln(2h/a) per unit length. A 5 mm radius wire 5 m up gives about 7.3 pF/m.
- Two parallel wires of radius a, separation d ≫ a: C′ ≈ πε₀/ln(d/a).

Energy stored
- Charging a capacitor from 0 to V takes W = ∫ V dQ = ½CV² = ½QV = Q²/(2C). A 10 μF capacitor at 100 V stores 0.05 J.
- The energy can be regarded as stored in the field, with energy density w = ½ D · E = ½εE² (J/m³). For a parallel-plate capacitor, ½εE² × Ad = ½(εA/d)V².

Effect of dielectrics
- Insert a dielectric into a capacitor held at constant voltage: C and the stored energy both rise by εr, and the supply provides extra charge.
- Insert it into an isolated (constant-charge) capacitor: C rises by εr, V falls by εr and the stored energy falls by εr; the dielectric is pulled in.

Virtual work
- To find a force, imagine a small displacement dx and balance energy.
- Constant charge (isolated): no electrical input, so F dx = −dW, F = −dW/dx.
- Constant voltage (connected to a supply): the supply delivers V dQ = V² dC, of which half goes into stored energy, so F = +½V² dC/dx. This is the version emphasised in the syllabus.
- Both give the same force for the same configuration.

Examples
- Parallel plates, C = εA/x: dC/dx = −εA/x², so F = −½εAV²/x², an attraction of magnitude ½εE²A. The "electrostatic pressure" is ½εE².
- Plates 0.01 m² in air, 1 mm apart, 1 kV: F = ½ × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 0.01 × (10⁶)² ≈ 0.044 N.
- Even at air's breakdown field of about 3 MV/m the pressure is only about 40 Pa. This is why electrostatic actuators are used at micro scale (MEMS) but magnetic actuators dominate in large machines.
- A dielectric slab partly inserted between plates (width w, gap d): C(x) = ε₀w[εr x + (l − x)]/d, so F = ½V²ε₀w(εr − 1)/d, pulling the slab in, independent of x.

Exam tips: state whether V or Q is held constant before differentiating; the sign of the force comes from physical sense (charges attract, dielectrics are drawn into high-field regions).

Why magnetic materials?
Air-cored coils need enormous currents to make useful fields. Ferromagnetic materials such as iron multiply the flux density for a given current by a large factor, which is why motors, transformers and electromagnets use iron cores.

Magnetic field H and permeability
- H (A/m) is defined so that Ampère's law involves only the free (conduction) current: ∮ H · dl = NI, the magnetomotive force (MMF), in ampere-turns.
- In a linear material B = μ₀μrH, where μr is the relative permeability: about 1 for air and copper, and of order thousands for soft iron and electrical steels.

Magnetic circuits
- In a core of length l, area A and permeability μ₀μr carrying flux Φ: H = Φ/(μ₀μrA), so the MMF needed is Hl = Φ × l/(μ₀μrA).
- Define reluctance S = l/(μ₀μrA) (A/Wb). Then MMF = ΦS, the magnetic analogue of V = IR: MMF ↔ emf, flux ↔ current, reluctance ↔ resistance.
- Reluctances in series add; flux is continuous round the circuit (the analogue of Kirchhoff's current law).
- Inductance of an N-turn coil on the core: L = N²/S.

Air gaps dominate
Because μr for iron is large, a short air gap often has far more reluctance than the whole iron path. For an iron path of 0.2 m with μr = 1000 and a 0.5 mm gap, the gap's reluctance is proportional to 0.5 × 10⁻³ m against 0.2/1000 = 0.2 × 10⁻³ m for the iron (each divided by the same μ₀A): the gap dominates.

Worked example
Core area 4 cm², iron path 0.2 m (μr = 1000), gap 0.5 mm, 200 turns. Current for B = 1 T in the gap (ignoring fringing)?
- H_gap = B/μ₀ ≈ 7.96 × 10⁵ A/m; MMF_gap ≈ 7.96 × 10⁵ × 0.5 × 10⁻³ ≈ 398 A.
- H_iron = B/(μ₀μr) ≈ 796 A/m; MMF_iron ≈ 159 A.
- Total ≈ 557 A-turns, so I ≈ 557/200 ≈ 2.8 A. Inductance L = NΦ/I = 200 × 4 × 10⁻⁴/2.79 ≈ 29 mH.

Non-linear behaviour
- Ferromagnets contain domains, regions of aligned atomic moments. Applying H grows favourably aligned domains and rotates others, giving large B.
- The B–H (magnetisation) curve is non-linear: μr is not constant, and above a certain flux density the material saturates (for electrical steels typically somewhere around 1.5–2 T), after which B rises only slowly, with dB/dH close to μ₀, as if the material were air.
- On cycling, B lags H: a hysteresis loop. Remanence Br is the B left at H = 0; coercivity Hc is the reverse H needed to bring B to zero.
- The area of the loop is the energy lost per unit volume per cycle (hysteresis loss). Soft materials (narrow loops) suit AC cores; hard materials (wide loops) make permanent magnets.
- Changing flux also induces eddy currents in a conducting core; laminating the core reduces them.

Transformers
The 2025–26 syllabus lists transformers with a question mark, so check whether they are lectured this year.
- Two windings on a shared core link the same flux. For an ideal transformer V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂, I₁/I₂ = N₂/N₁, and an impedance Z on the secondary appears as (N₁/N₂)²Z at the primary.
- Real transformers draw a magnetising current and suffer copper, hysteresis and eddy-current losses.

Exam tips: build an "equivalent circuit" of reluctances and solve it like a resistor network; then check whether the resulting B would saturate the iron.

notes.h: Permanent magnets, magnetic energy and forces
notes.body:
Magnetic energy
- Building up a current in an inductor stores W = ½LI². For a linear magnetic circuit this equals ½ΦF where F is the MMF.
- In general the energy stored per unit volume when B is raised is ∫ H dB. For a linear material this gives w = ½BH = B²/(2μ₀μr).
- Because μr is large in iron, almost all the energy in a gapped magnetic circuit is stored in the air gap.
- At 1 T in air, w = 1/(2 × 4π × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4 × 10⁵ J/m³.

Check on the circuit from the previous topic (4 cm², 0.2 m iron at μr = 1000, 0.5 mm gap, B = 1 T): gap energy ≈ 4 × 10⁵ × (4 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.5 × 10⁻³) ≈ 0.080 J; iron energy ≈ (4 × 10⁵/1000) × (4 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.2) ≈ 0.032 J; total ≈ 0.11 J, matching ½LI² = ½ × 0.0287 × 2.79² ≈ 0.11 J.

Forces by virtual work
- At constant flux (no change in linkage, no electrical input): F = −dW/dx.
- At constant current: F = +½I² dL/dx.
- Both give the same answer. Applying either to an air gap of area A gives an attractive force F = B²A/(2μ₀) per pole face: the magnetic "pressure" is B²/(2μ₀).
- At 1 T the pressure is about 4 × 10⁵ Pa (roughly 4 atmospheres), so a 10 cm² pole face pulls with about 400 N. Compare with the ~40 Pa limit for electrostatic pressure in air: this is why practical actuators and motors are magnetic.
- Because B ∝ 1/(gap) for a gap-dominated circuit at fixed current, the force rises sharply as the gap closes.

Permanent magnets
- A permanent magnet uses a hard magnetic material with high remanence Br and high coercivity Hc. Common types include ferrites, alnico, samarium–cobalt and neodymium–iron–boron (NdFeB, with Br typically above 1 T).
- In a circuit with no winding, Ampère's law gives H_m l_m + H_g l_g = 0, so the magnet operates with negative H (in the second quadrant of its B–H loop, the "demagnetisation curve").
- Flux continuity (ignoring leakage and fringing) gives B_m A_m = B_g A_g.
- Combining these gives a load line, B_m = −μ₀(A_g/A_m)(l_m/l_g)H_m. The operating point is where it meets the demagnetisation curve.
- For a minimum volume of magnet, design so that the operating point is at the maximum energy product (BH)max.

Worked example
A magnet with a straight-line demagnetisation curve B = Br + μ₀H_m (recoil permeability approximately μ₀), Br = 1.2 T, length 10 mm, drives flux through a 2 mm gap of equal area (iron reluctance neglected). Then H_m = −B l_g/(μ₀l_m), so B = Br − B(l_g/l_m), giving B = Br/(1 + l_g/l_m) = 1.2/1.2 = 1.0 T.

Exam tips: in force questions, find B in the gap first from the magnetic circuit, then use B²A/(2μ₀) per gap face; remember a U-shaped electromagnet lifting a bar has two gaps.

cards.b: F = q₁q₂/(4πεr²) along the line between two point charges; like charges repel. In vacuum ε = ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m.

cards.f: Electric field of an infinite line charge λ
cards.b: E = λ/(2πεr), radial, falling as 1/r.

cards.f: Electric field of an infinite sheet σ
cards.b: E = σ/(2ε) on each side, independent of distance from the sheet.
Small displacement of bound charge (or alignment of molecular dipoles) by the applied field, giving surface polarisation charge that reduces E inside.
Ratio ε/ε₀; a linear dielectric filling all the space around given free charges reduces the field and force between them by εr.
Above the dielectric strength an insulator conducts (e.g. ionisation avalanche); about 3 MV/m for air at atmospheric pressure.
The field of several charges is the vector sum of the fields of each charge acting alone.
∮ D · dS = free charge enclosed: the net flux of D out of a closed surface equals the enclosed free charge.
D = εE = ε₀εrE in a linear dielectric; generally D = ε₀E + P. D depends only on free charge.

cards.f: Boundary condition on D (no free surface charge)
cards.b: The normal component of D is continuous, so E is larger in the lower-permittivity layer.
V_A − V_B = ∫ from A to B of E · dl; equivalently E = −∇V.
V = (λ/2πε) ln(b/a) for radii a < b with λ per unit length.

cards.f: Field inside a conductor in equilibrium
cards.b: Zero; any net charge resides on the surface.
C = 4πε₀R.
C = εA/d, neglecting fringing.
C′ = 2πε/ln(b/a).
1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂; same charge on each, voltages add.
i = C dv/dt; voltage cannot change instantaneously.
Z = 1/(jωC); reactance 1/(ωC); current leads voltage by 90°.

cards.f: Two dielectric layers in series: which is most stressed?
cards.b: D is equal in both, so E = D/ε is largest in the layer with the lowest permittivity (often an air gap).
Current per unit area (A/m²); J = nqv_d for n carriers of charge q with drift velocity v_d.
J = σE, with conductivity σ = 1/ρ.
R = ρL/A.
R = ρ ln(b/a)/(2πl) for length l.

cards.f: Product RC for the same geometry
cards.b: RC = ρε, because the field problem for current flow and for capacitance is the same.
About 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m at room temperature.

cards.f: Force per unit length between parallel wires
cards.b: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd); attractive for currents in the same direction.
F = I L × B; magnitude BIL when the wire is perpendicular to B.
dB = μ₀I dl × r̂/(4πr²): the field of a short current element.

cards.f: B near a long straight wire
cards.b: B = μ₀I/(2πr), circulating (right-hand grip rule).

cards.f: B at the centre of a circular loop
cards.b: B = μ₀I/(2a) for a single turn of radius a.
B = μ₀nI, uniform and axial, with n turns per metre; approximately zero outside.
∮ B · dl = μ₀ × current enclosed by the loop.

cards.f: B inside a solid wire of radius a
cards.b: B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²), rising linearly from zero at the centre.
e = −dλ/dt = −N dΦ/dt; the minus sign (Lenz's law) means the induced current opposes the change.
λ = NΦ for N turns each linking flux Φ.
L = λ/I; then v = L di/dt.
L = μ₀N²A/l.
M = λ₂/I₁ = λ₁/I₂ (M₁₂ = M₂₁); M = k√(L₁L₂) with coupling coefficient k.
Z = jωL; reactance ωL; current lags voltage by 90°.
e = Blv for a conductor of length l moving at v perpendicular to B.
L′C′ = μ₀ε, independent of the radii.
Replace the plane by an equal and opposite charge at the mirror point; the field on the real side is unchanged.

cards.f: Force on point charge q at height h above a grounded plane
cards.b: Attractive, q²/(4πε₀(2h)²).

cards.f: Capacitance per unit length of a wire above ground
cards.b: C′ ≈ 2πε₀/ln(2h/a) for radius a at height h ≫ a.
W = ½CV² = ½QV = Q²/(2C).
w = ½D · E = ½εE² (J/m³).

cards.f: Virtual work force at constant voltage
cards.b: F = +½V² dC/dx.
½εE², about 40 Pa in air even at the ~3 MV/m breakdown field.

cards.f: Ampère's law in terms of H
cards.b: ∮ H · dl = NI (the MMF, in ampere-turns).
S = l/(μ₀μrA); MMF = ΦS, the magnetic analogue of V = IR.
L = N²/S.

cards.f: Why air gaps dominate magnetic circuits
cards.b: μr of iron is in the thousands, so a gap of length g has the same reluctance as roughly μr × g of iron.
Above a certain flux density (around 1.5–2 T for electrical steels) nearly all domains are aligned and B rises only slowly, with dB/dH close to μ₀.
Br: B remaining at H = 0; Hc: reverse H needed to reduce B to zero.
Energy lost per unit volume per cycle equals the area of the B–H loop.

cards.f: Purpose of laminating a transformer core
cards.b: To break up eddy-current paths and so reduce eddy-current losses.
w = ½BH = B²/(2μ₀μr); in general ∫ H dB per unit volume.

cards.f: Force across an air gap of area A
cards.b: F = B²A/(2μ₀) per pole face (magnetic pressure B²/(2μ₀)).
About 4 × 10⁵ Pa.

cards.f: Virtual work force at constant current
cards.b: F = +½I² dL/dx.

cards.f: Where does a permanent magnet operate on its B–H loop?
cards.b: In the second quadrant (B positive, H negative): the demagnetisation curve.

cards.f: Load line of a magnet with an air gap
cards.b: B_m = −μ₀(A_g/A_m)(l_m/l_g)H_m, from H_m l_m + H_g l_g = 0 and B_m A_m = B_g A_g.

cards.f: Design criterion for minimum magnet volume
cards.b: Operate at the maximum energy product (BH)max.

questions.q: What is the magnitude of the electric field 0.3 m from a 2 nC point charge in air?
questions.why: E = Q/(4πε₀r²) = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁹/0.09 ≈ 200 V/m. 60 V/m uses 1/r instead of 1/r²; 600 V/m divides by 0.03; 2 × 10⁵ V/m treats the charge as 2 μC instead of 2 nC.

questions.q: How does the field of a uniformly charged, very long straight line vary with perpendicular distance r?
questions.why: By Gauss's law on a coaxial cylinder, E × 2πrl = λl/ε, so E = λ/(2πεr) ∝ 1/r. Independence of r is the infinite sheet, 1/r² the point charge and 1/r³ the far field of a dipole.

questions.q: Point charges of +4 μC and +1 μC are fixed 0.3 m apart in air. (a) Find the force between them. (b) Find where on the line between them the electric field is zero.
markScheme: F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²) with correct substitution
F ≈ 0.40 N, repulsive
Sets fields equal: 4/x² = 1/(0.3 − x)²
Takes the root between the charges: 2(0.3 − x) = x
x = 0.2 m from the 4 μC charge (0.1 m from the 1 μC charge)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) F = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻⁶ × 1 × 10⁻⁶/0.3² = 0.0360/0.09 ≈ 0.40 N, repulsive because both charges are positive. (b) Between the charges the two fields point in opposite directions, so the null is where their magnitudes are equal: 4/x² = 1/(0.3 − x)². Taking square roots (both distances positive), 2(0.3 − x) = x, so x = 0.2 m. The null is 0.2 m from the 4 μC charge and 0.1 m from the 1 μC charge, closer to the smaller charge as expected.

questions.q: A capacitor has a 1 mm layer of glass (εr = 6) in series with a 0.1 mm air gap between its plates. In which layer is the electric field strength E greater, and by what factor?
options: They are equal, because the layers are in series
questions.why: With no free charge on the interface, D is the same in both layers, so E = D/ε is six times larger in the air (εr = 1) than in the glass (εr = 6). The thickness ratio of 10 affects the voltage share, not the field ratio; series layers share D, not E.

questions.q: What is the capacitance of an isolated conducting sphere of radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m (Earth-sized) in a vacuum?
questions.why: C = 4πε₀R = 4π × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 6.37 × 10⁶ ≈ 7.1 × 10⁻⁴ F. The other options are power-of-ten errors; the point is how small free-space capacitances are.

questions.q: A coaxial cable has inner conductor radius a and outer conductor inner radius b, with dielectric of permittivity ε between them. Using Gauss's law, find the electric field at radius r (a < r < b) when the inner conductor carries charge λ per unit length, and hence derive the capacitance per unit length.
markScheme: Chooses a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length l, with D radial by symmetry and no flux through the ends
D × 2πrl = λl, so D = λ/(2πr) and E = λ/(2πεr)
V = ∫ from a to b of E dr = (λ/2πε) ln(b/a)
C′ = λ/V = 2πε/ln(b/a)
States assumptions (infinitely long, end effects ignored)
questions.modelAnswer: By symmetry D is radial and depends only on r. Take a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length l coaxial with the cable. Only the curved surface carries flux, so D × 2πrl = λl and D = λ/(2πr), giving E = λ/(2πεr) for a < r < b. The voltage between conductors is V = ∫ from a to b of λ/(2πεr) dr = (λ/2πε) ln(b/a). The capacitance per unit length is C′ = λ/V = 2πε/ln(b/a). This assumes a long cable so end effects can be ignored.

questions.q: Parallel plates of area 0.01 m² are separated by 0.1 mm of dielectric with εr = 4. What is the capacitance?
questions.why: C = ε₀εrA/d = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 4 × 0.01/10⁻⁴ ≈ 3.54 × 10⁻⁹ F = 3.5 nF. 0.89 nF omits εr; 35 nF and 3.5 pF are power-of-ten slips in d or the prefix.

questions.q: A sinusoidal voltage is applied across an ideal capacitor and the frequency is doubled with the amplitude unchanged. What happens to the current amplitude and its phase relative to the voltage?
options: Current is unchanged; it is in phase
questions.why: I = jωCV, so the current amplitude ωCV doubles with ω and the factor j means the current leads the voltage by 90°. Lagging by 90° describes an inductor; in-phase describes a resistor.

questions.q: Plates of area 0.01 m² have 1 mm of glass (εr = 6) and a 0.1 mm air gap in series between them, with 1 kV applied. Find the field in each layer and comment on the risk of breakdown.
markScheme: Recognises series layers with equal D (or uses series capacitances)
Writes V = D(d_glass/ε_glass + d_air/ε₀) or equivalent
E_air ≈ 3.75 MV/m and E_glass ≈ 0.63 MV/m
Notes E_air exceeds the ~3 MV/m breakdown strength of air, so the gap may discharge
questions.modelAnswer: D is the same in both layers. Then V = E_glass d_glass + E_air d_air = D(d_glass/(6ε₀) + d_air/ε₀) = (D/ε₀)(10⁻³/6 + 10⁻⁴) = (D/ε₀)(2.667 × 10⁻⁴). With V = 1000 V, D/ε₀ = 3.75 × 10⁶ V/m, so E_air = 3.75 MV/m and E_glass = 3.75/6 ≈ 0.63 MV/m (D ≈ 3.32 × 10⁻⁵ C/m²). Check: 375 V across the air and 625 V across the glass. The air gap field exceeds the roughly 3 MV/m breakdown strength of air, so the gap is likely to suffer partial discharge even though the glass is lightly stressed.

questions.q: A copper wire is drawn out to twice its original length at constant volume. By what factor does its resistance change?
questions.why: At constant volume, doubling L halves A, so R = ρL/A rises by 2 × 2 = 4. ×2 ignores the reduced area; ×½ and unchanged have no basis.

questions.q: The space between two coaxial cylinders (radii a < b, length l) is filled with a weakly conducting material of resistivity ρ and permittivity ε. Which expression gives the product of the leakage resistance and the capacitance?
questions.why: R = ρ ln(b/a)/(2πl) and C = 2πεl/ln(b/a), so RC = ρε: the geometry cancels because the same field pattern governs both problems. Expressions that keep ln(b/a) or l have failed to cancel the geometry, and ρ/ε does not even have units of time.

questions.q: A 1 mm² copper wire carries 1 A. Copper has about 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³ and resistivity 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. Find (a) the current density, (b) the electron drift speed, (c) the electric field in the wire.
markScheme: J = I/A = 10⁶ A/m²
v_d = J/(nq) ≈ 7 × 10⁻⁵ m/s
Comments that drift speed is tiny compared with signal speed
questions.modelAnswer: (a) J = I/A = 1/10⁻⁶ = 10⁶ A/m². (b) J = nqv_d, so v_d = 10⁶/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 7.4 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, less than a tenth of a millimetre per second. (c) E = ρJ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ × 10⁶ = 0.017 V/m. Electrons drift very slowly; electrical signals travel quickly because the field is established along the wire almost at once.

questions.q: What is the magnetic flux density 5 cm from a long straight wire carrying 10 A in air?
questions.why: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10/0.05 = 4 × 10⁻⁵ T = 40 μT. 4 and 400 μT are factor-of-ten slips; 126 μT uses the loop-centre formula μ₀I/(2r) instead of the straight-wire result.

questions.q: Two long parallel wires 1 m apart each carry 100 A in opposite directions. What is the force on each per metre length?
questions.why: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 100 × 100/1 = 2 × 10⁻³ N/m. Currents in opposite directions repel; same-direction currents attract.

questions.q: A long solid cylindrical conductor of radius a carries current I distributed uniformly over its cross-section. Use Ampère's law to find B inside and outside the conductor and sketch B against r.
markScheme: By symmetry B is circumferential and constant on a circle of radius r
Outside (r > a): B × 2πr = μ₀I, B = μ₀I/(2πr)
Inside: enclosed current I r²/a²
B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²) for r < a
Sketch: linear rise to μ₀I/(2πa) at r = a, then 1/r decay
questions.modelAnswer: By symmetry B circles the axis and has constant magnitude on any coaxial circle of radius r, so ∮ B · dl = 2πrB. Outside (r > a) the whole current is enclosed: 2πrB = μ₀I, so B = μ₀I/(2πr). Inside (r < a) the enclosed current is I × πr²/πa² = Ir²/a², so 2πrB = μ₀Ir²/a² and B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²). B rises linearly from zero at the axis to μ₀I/(2πa) at the surface, then falls as 1/r.

questions.q: A 100-turn coil of area 0.01 m² sits in a uniform field normal to its plane that rises steadily from 0 to 0.5 T in 0.1 s. What emf is induced?
questions.why: e = N dΦ/dt = 100 × 0.01 × 0.5/0.1 = 5 V. 0.05 V omits N; 0.5 V and 50 V are factor-of-ten slips.

questions.q: A long air-cored solenoid has its number of turns doubled while its length and cross-section stay the same. Its inductance:
questions.why: L = μ₀N²A/l: doubling N doubles B for a given current and doubles the number of turns linking it, so L rises by a factor of 4.

questions.q: A long solenoid has 2000 turns per metre and cross-sectional area 10⁻³ m². A 50-turn coil is wound tightly around its middle. (a) Find the mutual inductance. (b) The solenoid carries i = 3 sin(100πt) A. Find the amplitude of the emf induced in the coil.
markScheme: B inside solenoid = μ₀n₁i
Flux linkage of coil = N₂μ₀n₁iA, so M = μ₀n₁N₂A
e = M di/dt, amplitude ωMÎ
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Inside the solenoid B = μ₀n₁i, uniform over area A. The coil links λ = N₂BA = μ₀n₁N₂A i, so M = μ₀n₁N₂A = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 × 50 × 10⁻³ ≈ 1.26 × 10⁻⁴ H (126 μH). (b) e = M di/dt = M × 3 × 100π cos(100πt), so the amplitude is 1.26 × 10⁻⁴ × 300π ≈ 0.12 V.

questions.q: A point charge of 1 nC is held 1 cm above a large grounded conducting plane. What is the force on it?
options: About 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ N away from the plane
Zero, because the plane is earthed
questions.why: The image is −1 nC at 1 cm below the plane, 2 cm from the charge. F = q²/(4πε₀(2h)²) = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 10⁻¹⁸/(0.02)² ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ N, attractive. 9 × 10⁻⁵ N uses h instead of 2h; the force is not repulsive; earthing the plane is what makes the induced charge appear.

questions.q: A capacitor is charged, disconnected from the supply, and then a dielectric slab (εr = 3) is inserted to fill the gap. The stored energy:
questions.why: With Q fixed, W = Q²/(2C) and C triples, so W falls to a third; the lost energy is the work done pulling the slab in. If the supply had stayed connected (V fixed), W = ½CV² would triple instead.

questions.q: Parallel plates of area A are separated by a variable gap x in air and held at constant voltage V. (a) Use virtual work to derive the force between them. (b) Evaluate it for A = 0.01 m², x = 1 mm, V = 1 kV. (c) Explain why electrostatic actuators are rarely used at large scale.
markScheme: Constant-V virtual work: F = ½V² dC/dx
C = ε₀A/x, dC/dx = −ε₀A/x²
F = −ε₀AV²/(2x²), attractive (magnitude ½ε₀E²A)
Numerical value ≈ 0.044 N
Pressure limited by breakdown (~3 MV/m in air) to about 40 Pa, much less than magnetic pressure B²/(2μ₀)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) At constant voltage the supply delivers V dQ = V² dC when the plates move by dx, of which half is stored (d(½CV²) = ½V² dC), so the mechanical work is F dx = ½V² dC, F = ½V² dC/dx. With C = ε₀A/x, dC/dx = −ε₀A/x², so F = −ε₀AV²/(2x²): an attraction (tending to reduce x) of magnitude ½ε₀E²A where E = V/x. (b) F = ½ × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 0.01 × (10³/10⁻³)² ≈ 0.044 N. (c) The pressure ½ε₀E² is capped by breakdown: at about 3 MV/m in air it is only about 40 Pa, against about 4 × 10⁵ Pa for a magnetic gap at 1 T. Electrostatic forces only become competitive at micro scale (MEMS), where gaps are tiny.

questions.q: A magnetic circuit has an iron path of 0.2 m (μr = 1000) and an air gap of 0.5 mm, both of the same cross-section. Approximately what fraction of the total MMF is needed for the air gap?
questions.why: Reluctance ∝ l/μr: iron 0.2/1000 = 0.2 mm equivalent, gap 0.5 mm. The gap takes 0.5/(0.5 + 0.2) ≈ 71% of the MMF. 29% is the iron's share; 50% and 99% do not follow from the numbers.

questions.q: An 8 Ω loudspeaker is connected to the secondary of an ideal transformer with turns ratio N₁:N₂ = 10:1. What resistance is seen at the primary?
questions.why: A load Z on the secondary appears as (N₁/N₂)²Z = 100 × 8 = 800 Ω at the primary. 80 Ω uses the turns ratio without squaring it; 0.08 Ω inverts the ratio.

questions.q: A core has cross-section 4 cm², an iron path of 0.2 m with μr = 1000, an air gap of 0.5 mm and a 200-turn winding. Ignoring fringing and leakage, find the current needed for 1 T in the gap and the inductance of the winding.
markScheme: Φ = BA = 4 × 10⁻⁴ Wb, same in iron and gap
MMF_iron = (B/μ₀μr) × 0.2 ≈ 159 A
L = NΦ/I (or N²/S) ≈ 29 mH
questions.modelAnswer: Φ = BA = 1 × 4 × 10⁻⁴ = 4 × 10⁻⁴ Wb, the same in iron and gap. Gap: H = B/μ₀ ≈ 7.96 × 10⁵ A/m, MMF ≈ 7.96 × 10⁵ × 0.5 × 10⁻³ ≈ 398 A-turns. Iron: H = B/(μ₀μr) ≈ 796 A/m, MMF ≈ 796 × 0.2 ≈ 159 A-turns. Total ≈ 557 A-turns, so I ≈ 557/200 ≈ 2.8 A. Inductance L = NΦ/I = 200 × 4 × 10⁻⁴/2.79 ≈ 0.029 H (29 mH); equivalently N²/S with S = 557/(4 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.39 × 10⁶ A/Wb.

questions.q: What is the attractive force across one pole face of area 10 cm² when the gap flux density is 1 T?
questions.why: F = B²A/(2μ₀) = 1 × 10⁻³/(2 × 4π × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 398 N. 800 N would be two pole faces; 40 N and 4000 N are factor-of-ten slips (e.g. in converting cm² to m²).

questions.q: A permanent magnet with a straight-line demagnetisation curve B = Br + μ₀H (Br = 1.2 T) and length 10 mm drives flux through a 2 mm air gap of the same area, with the iron reluctance negligible. What is the gap flux density?
questions.why: Ampère: H_m l_m + (B/μ₀) l_g = 0, so H_m = −B l_g/(μ₀ l_m). Substituting: B = Br − B(l_g/l_m) = Br − 0.2B, so B = 1.2/1.2 = 1.0 T. 1.2 T ignores the demagnetising effect of the gap; 0.2 T and 0.6 T do not satisfy both equations.

questions.q: Show that the energy stored per unit volume in a linear magnetic material is B²/(2μ₀μr), and use this to explain why almost all the energy in a gapped iron-cored inductor is stored in the gap.
markScheme: Energy per unit volume = ∫ H dB
With H = B/(μ₀μr) this gives B²/(2μ₀μr)
Flux continuity gives the same B in iron and gap (same area)
Energy per unit volume in iron is 1/μr of that in the gap
Unless the iron path is longer than μr times the gap length, the gap holds most of the energy
questions.modelAnswer: Raising the flux density by dB in unit volume requires energy H dB, so w = ∫ H dB. In a linear material H = B/(μ₀μr), so w = ∫ from 0 to B of B′/(μ₀μr) dB′ = B²/(2μ₀μr). In a gapped core of uniform cross-section the flux, and hence B, is the same in iron and gap. The energy density in the iron is therefore 1/μr of that in the gap. With μr in the thousands, the iron stores only a small fraction of the total unless its path length exceeds roughly μr times the gap length. For example, 0.2 m of iron at μr = 1000 and a 0.5 mm gap store energy in the ratio 0.2/1000 : 0.5 × 10⁻³, i.e. 0.2 : 0.5, so the gap holds about 71%.

questions.q:
A coaxial cable has an inner conductor of radius a = 1 mm and an outer conductor of inner radius b = 4 mm. The space between is filled with polyethylene, εr = 2.25, μr = 1. The cable is 100 m long.
(a) Using Gauss's law, derive an expression for the electric field at radius r between the conductors when the voltage between them is V. [5]
(b) Find the capacitance of the cable. [3]
(c) Find the maximum electric field in the dielectric when V = 10 kV, and state where it occurs. [3]
(d) Show that, for a fixed outer radius b and voltage V, the maximum field is minimised when b/a = e. [4]
(e) Using Ampère's law, derive the inductance per unit length (neglecting flux inside the conductors), find the inductance of the cable, and show that L′C′ = μ₀ε. [5]
markScheme: (a) Cylindrical Gaussian surface: D = λ/(2πr), E = λ/(2πεr); V = (λ/2πε) ln(b/a), so E(r) = V/(r ln(b/a))
(b) C′ = 2πε/ln(b/a) ≈ 90.3 pF/m; C ≈ 9.0 nF for 100 m
(c) E_max at r = a: V/(a ln(b/a)) ≈ 7.2 MV/m
(d) E_max = V/f(a) is minimised when f(a) = a ln(b/a) is maximised: df/da = ln(b/a) − 1 = 0, so b/a = e; checks it is a maximum of f
(e) Ampère: B = μ₀I/(2πr) for a < r < b; flux per unit length = (μ₀I/2π) ln(b/a)
L′ = (μ₀/2π) ln(b/a) ≈ 0.277 μH/m; L ≈ 27.7 μH for 100 m
L′C′ = (μ₀/2π) ln(b/a) × 2πε/ln(b/a) = μ₀ε; comments that 1/√(L′C′) = c/√εr ≈ 2 × 10⁸ m/s is the signal speed
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let the inner conductor carry charge λ per unit length. By symmetry D is radial. A coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r (a < r < b) and length l encloses λl, and only its curved face carries flux, so D × 2πrl = λl, D = λ/(2πr) and E = λ/(2πεr) with ε = 2.25ε₀. The voltage is V = ∫ from a to b of E dr = (λ/2πε) ln(b/a). Eliminating λ: E(r) = V/(r ln(b/a)).

(b) C′ = λ/V = 2πε/ln(b/a) = 2π × 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 2.25/ln 4 = 1.252 × 10⁻¹⁰/1.386 ≈ 9.03 × 10⁻¹¹ F/m (90.3 pF/m). For 100 m, C ≈ 9.0 nF.

(c) E ∝ 1/r, so it is greatest at the surface of the inner conductor, r = a: E_max = V/(a ln(b/a)) = 10⁴/(10⁻³ × 1.386) ≈ 7.2 × 10⁶ V/m (7.2 MV/m).

(d) E_max = V/f(a) with f(a) = a ln(b/a). For fixed V and b, E_max is smallest when f is largest. df/da = ln(b/a) + a × (−1/a) = ln(b/a) − 1, which is zero when ln(b/a) = 1, i.e. b/a = e. d²f/da² = −1/a < 0, so this is a maximum of f and hence a minimum of E_max. (Physically, a thinner inner conductor has a higher surface field, but a fatter one leaves too little dielectric thickness.)

(e) With current I in the inner conductor and −I returning in the outer, Ampère's law on a circle of radius r between the conductors gives B × 2πr = μ₀I, so B = μ₀I/(2πr); outside the cable B = 0. The flux crossing a strip of unit length between r = a and r = b is Φ′ = ∫ from a to b of μ₀I/(2πr) dr = (μ₀I/2π) ln(b/a). This flux links the current once, so L′ = Φ′/I = (μ₀/2π) ln(b/a) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.386 ≈ 2.77 × 10⁻⁷ H/m, and L ≈ 27.7 μH for 100 m. Multiplying, L′C′ = (μ₀/2π) ln(b/a) × 2πε/ln(b/a) = μ₀ε, independent of the radii. The quantity 1/√(L′C′) = 1/√(μ₀ε) = c/√εr ≈ 3 × 10⁸/1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed at which signals travel along the cable.

questions.q:
An electromagnet consists of a C-shaped iron core of uniform cross-section 25 cm² with a mean iron path length of 0.4 m and a single air gap of 2 mm. The iron has μr = 2000 (assume linear) and the winding has 500 turns. Neglect leakage and fringing.
(a) Calculate the reluctance of the iron and of the gap. [4]
(b) Find the winding current needed to give a flux density of 0.8 T in the gap. [4]
(c) Find the inductance of the winding and the stored magnetic energy at this current. [4]
(d) Use the principle of virtual work to find the force tending to close the gap. [5]
(e) Explain how the real behaviour would differ if the iron were driven to 1.8 T, and why the core of an AC electromagnet is laminated. [3]
markScheme: (a) S_iron = l/(μ₀μrA) ≈ 6.37 × 10⁴ A/Wb; S_gap = g/(μ₀A) ≈ 6.37 × 10⁵ A/Wb
(b) Φ = BA = 2 × 10⁻³ Wb; MMF = Φ(S_iron + S_gap) ≈ 1401 A-turns; I ≈ 2.80 A
(c) L = N²/S_total ≈ 0.357 H; W = ½LI² ≈ 1.40 J (or ½ΦF)
(d) At constant flux, W = ½Φ²S and dS/dg = 1/(μ₀A); F = −dW/dg gives magnitude Φ²/(2μ₀A) = B²A/(2μ₀)
(d) F ≈ 637 N, acting to close the gap
(e) Saturation: μr falls sharply, so much more current is needed and the linear model underestimates I; B cannot rise much above saturation
(e) Laminations break eddy-current paths, reducing eddy-current loss and heating (hysteresis loss also occurs)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) μ₀A = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2.5 × 10⁻³ = 3.142 × 10⁻⁹ H m. S_iron = l/(μ₀μrA) = 0.4/(2000 × 3.142 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 6.37 × 10⁴ A/Wb. S_gap = g/(μ₀A) = 2 × 10⁻³/3.142 × 10⁻⁹ ≈ 6.37 × 10⁵ A/Wb. The 2 mm gap has ten times the reluctance of 0.4 m of iron.

(b) Φ = BA = 0.8 × 2.5 × 10⁻³ = 2 × 10⁻³ Wb (the same in iron and gap, as there is no leakage or fringing). Total reluctance ≈ 7.00 × 10⁵ A/Wb, so MMF = ΦS = 2 × 10⁻³ × 7.00 × 10⁵ ≈ 1401 A-turns (about 1273 for the gap and 127 for the iron). I = 1401/500 ≈ 2.80 A.

(c) L = N²/S = 500²/7.00 × 10⁵ ≈ 0.357 H. W = ½LI² = ½ × 0.357 × 2.80² ≈ 1.40 J. Check: ½ΦF = ½ × 2 × 10⁻³ × 1401 ≈ 1.40 J, of which the gap holds B²/(2μ₀) × A g = 2.546 × 10⁵ × 5 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 1.27 J.

(d) Hold the flux constant and let the gap increase by dg. No emf is induced, so no electrical energy enters, and the mechanical work done by the magnetic force equals the decrease in stored energy: F dg = −dW. With W = ½Φ²S and S = S_iron + g/(μ₀A), dW/dg = ½Φ²/(μ₀A). Hence F = −Φ²/(2μ₀A): an attraction, tending to close the gap, of magnitude Φ²/(2μ₀A) = B²A/(2μ₀) = 0.64 × 2.5 × 10⁻³/(2 × 4π × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 637 N. (The constant-current method, F = ½I² dL/dg, gives the same result.)

(e) At 1.8 T a typical electrical steel is near or in saturation: its incremental permeability falls dramatically, so the iron's reluctance is no longer negligible and much more current is needed than the linear model predicts; B can then rise only slowly with further current. In an AC electromagnet the alternating flux induces eddy currents in the conducting core, which waste power and heat it; building the core from thin insulated laminations breaks up the eddy-current paths and greatly reduces this loss. Hysteresis loss, proportional to the B–H loop area per cycle, also occurs.
